passages.t: The sanctuary and the Most Holy Place
passages.happening:
The man brought Ezekiel to the outer sanctuary of the temple and measured its entrance and the hall (verses 1-2). Then he went alone into the inner sanctuary and measured it, twenty cubits long and twenty wide, and said, “This is the Most Holy Place.” (verse 4).

He measured the walls and the three stories of side rooms around the temple, thirty rooms on each level, resting on ledges (verses 5-11), and a building on the west side (verse 12). The walls were paneled with wood and carved with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub with two faces, ‘the face of a man’ toward one palm tree and ‘the face of a young lion’ toward the other (verses 18-19). Inside stood a wooden altar, and the man said, “This is the table that is before the LORD.” (verse 22). The doors were double and carved like the walls (verses 23-26).
passages.hearers:
The proportions follow Solomon's temple. Solomon's main hall was forty cubits long and twenty wide, and the inner room a cube of twenty cubits, matching Ezekiel's measurements. Solomon's temple also had three stories of side rooms resting on ledges, and carved cherubim and palm trees. This plan of porch, hall and inner room was shared with temples in Syria and southern Turkey; what made Israel's temple different was the God who lived in it.

In Israel only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year on the Day of Atonement. Ezekiel honors that boundary: the guide goes in alone, and the prophet, though a priest, stays outside and hears it named. In Solomon's temple that room held the ark beneath two great cherubim. Ezekiel's vision mentions no ark and no lampstand, only the wooden altar called the table before the LORD.
passages.later: Solomon's inner sanctuary ‘was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high’ (1 Kings 6:20). Aaron was warned ‘not to enter freely into the Most Holy Place’ (Leviticus 16:2).
passages.asks: Ezekiel stood outside while the Most Holy Place was named. Ask what it means to approach a holy God. And ask whether you take his nearness for granted.
